content:
The Letter to Titus, written in Paul's name, quotes a prophet of Crete on his own people and then vouches for him: "One of them, a prophet of their own, said, 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, and idle gluttons.' This testimony is true" (Titus 1:12 to 13).[1] Logicians have long noticed the trap. If a Cretan says all Cretans always lie, can he be telling the truth?

Muslim writers cite the verse as an error in inspired scripture, and Christian writers answer that it is rhetoric. Both sides usually miss what the logic actually shows, and what the verse does show.

This article aims to provide context to the verse, insha'Allah, in five questions about its source, its logic and what it says of a whole people. The Quran's rule on judging peoples frames the last of them: "Nor let some women laugh at others: It may be that the (latter are better than the (former)" (49:11).[2]

The letter does not name him. The New American Bible, published by the Catholic bishops of the United States, does: the line is "quoted from Epimenides, a Cretan poet of the sixth century B.C."[3] Ancient tradition remembered Epimenides as a seer and religious teacher of Crete, and much of what was told of him is legend.

Quoting a pagan poet was not new for the New Testament. Paul's speech in Athens cites "some of your own poets" (Acts 17:28), and 1 Corinthians quotes a Greek proverb: "Evil companionships corrupt good morals" (1 Corinthians 15:33).[1] What sets Titus apart is the next sentence. The writer does not only quote the line; he declares it true.

The popular form of the argument runs: if every Cretan always lies, then this Cretan is lying, so the statement is false; but then the statement was true. That is the liar paradox, and Titus 1:12 is not quite it.

If "Cretans are always liars" is false, it follows only that some Cretan sometimes tells the truth. It does not follow that Epimenides is telling the truth now. The statement can be false without any contradiction, and if Epimenides is lying, it simply is false. What cannot be coherent is the claim taken strictly and declared true by a writer citing a Cretan as his witness, since a witness from a nation of liars proves nothing.

Muslims who use the verse should use the stronger form. The problem is the endorsement, and the logic only sharpens it.

Christian interpreters answer that "always liars" is a figure of speech, the way one calls a person "a liar" without meaning every word he says. Read that way, the logical difficulty disappears.

A harder question takes its place. The quotation goes on: "evil beasts, and idle gluttons." The letter applies a slur to a whole island, and then tells Titus to "reprove them sharply" (Titus 1:13).[1] Matthijs den Dulk's study for Cambridge University Press, Ethnic Stereotypes and the Letters of Paul, gives a whole chapter, "Lying Cretans", to the verse, and asks how Paul's letters drew on ethnic stereotypes and how they shaped later views of outsiders.[4]

John Granger Cook reads the verse in its ancient religious setting. Cretans told that Zeus had died and showed his tomb on the island, and other Greeks counted that claim as the Cretans' great lie. Cook argues that the line belongs to an oracle, so that "the truth value of 1,12 consequently depends on the oracle and not the human being", and he notes that Syriac scholars preserved the tradition about Zeus's death.[5]

The reading is learned and possible. Titus itself mentions no Zeus and no oracle. A defence that needs a background the text never gives is a reconstruction, and it should be offered as one.

Many scholars doubt that Paul wrote the letters to Timothy and Titus at all, and treat them as written later in his name. We set out that debate in who wrote the letters of Paul? Apostle of Doom weighs the letters to Timothy and Titus as Scripture in the letters of a man. On either view, a letter that Christians receive as Scripture declares a pagan's insult against a people to be "true".

That is the real weight of the verse. The logic is a puzzle that careful readers can resolve, but the endorsement of a slur on a whole nation is an ethical problem that rhetoric does not remove. The Quran forbids exactly that kind of judgement: "let not the hatred of others to you make you swerve to wrong and depart from justice. Be just: that is next to piety" (5:8).[2]

The bottom line

Titus 1:12 quotes Epimenides, a Cretan poet of the sixth century BC, calling Cretans "always liars, evil beasts, and idle gluttons", and the letter declares the testimony true. Strictly read, the line does not produce the liar paradox, since a false universal claim needs only one honest Cretan; the difficulty lies in a scripture endorsing it. Cook's oracle reading and the rhetorical reading each answer the logic, and neither removes the slur.

Muslims who cite the verse should argue from what it shows: an inspired text vouching for a stereotype of a whole people. The Quran sets the opposite rule, and asks believers to check every report before they act on it (49:6) and to judge each person, never a nation, by what he does.[2] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Titus 1:12 to 13; Acts 17:28; 1 Corinthians 15:33 (World English Bible).
  2. Quran 5:8; 49:6; 49:11, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. New American Bible, Revised Edition, note on Titus 1:12 (Washington, DC: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops).
  4. Matthijs den Dulk, "Lying Cretans", in Ethnic Stereotypes and the Letters of Paul (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2026), pp. 176–209, doi:10.1017/9781009718127.007.
  5. John Granger Cook, "Titus 1,12: Epimenides, Ancient Christian Scholars, Zeus's Death, and the Cretan Paradox", Zeitschrift für Antikes Christentum 25, no. 3 (2021), pp. 367–394, doi:10.1515/zac-2021-0032.
